best_season: Spring into early summer (roughly once SR-20 opens for the season through June) is often cited as the best window, since residual snow in the upper basin firms up the loose ground and eases travel; by mid-to-late summer the route becomes a loose scree ('kitty litter') and talus slog with more exposed rock. The peak is effectively inaccessible in winter, since SR-20 is gated and closed for the season (typically closed by early December, reopening in spring on a variable date — as late as mid/late June in years with major storm/rockslide damage, as in 2026).

Both ends of the calendar have been used. The first ascent was in July, so the line goes as a summer rock-and-snow route; the only recorded winter ascent was 13 March 2005. Late winter through early spring is the more attractive window: the couloir is filled and frozen, the lower rock band takes hooks, thin ice and turf instead of being bare compact slab, the bergschrund is filled in, and the slide alder on the approach has no foliage. Against that, the snowpack must be settled — the whole route sits under the summit cornices — and the Stetattle Creek ford is unpleasant in any month. Consult the NWAC West Slopes North forecast before committing. Note that the approach trail is presently closed by fire damage regardless of season.

access.closures: NPS North Cascades fire closures page, last updated August 28, 2026: 'Stetattle Creek Trail' is closed under long-term post-fire hazard closures ('hazards from falling dead trees and other ground hazards resulting from wildfires').

hazards: Loose rock in the gully gaining the East Ridge from the Chiwawa-Fortress col.
Exposed, unroped 4th-class climbing on the final summit pitch.
Cold, thigh-to-knee-deep river fords crossing the Chiwawa River drainage on the approach.
Same FR 6200 road-closure access issue as the Southwest Face route (extra ~7 miles of road-walking each way since 2026).
Rockfall from loose talus and scree on the southwest face gully, especially with other climbers above.
Steep snow slopes on the approach into early summer requiring ice axe self-arrest skills.
River/creek crossings and brushy, sometimes-indistinct trail sections lower on the approach.
A long additional road-walk (~7 miles each way) to reach Trinity Trailhead due to a 2026 storm-damage closure of FR 6200 beyond Atkinson Flat Campground.

best_season: Jul-Aug per a first-hand account of the route

hazards: Extremely loose rock, especially on the west side of #2 Gully. In 2001 a climber was struck and briefly pinned by a roughly 500-pound block that rolled out of the dirt near the base of the gully as he weighted it — he called it his closest call in the mountains and noted a broken leg up there could have meant a multi-day rescue.
Rockfall generated by your own party on the descent is the norm, not the exception; keep parties tight and helmets on.
Benightment is close to standard: twelve hours is an absolute minimum and documented ascents run past 11 p.m.
No reliable water above roughly 2,100 ft.
Wet conditions make the gully's mix of sand and polished rock unjustifiably dangerous.

best_season: Mazamas rates it 'B' difficulty in summer and fall and 'Not Allowed' in spring/winter; late-season ascents may find reduced snowfield steepness on the upper section.

Best attempted early-to-mid summer while the Ruth and Icy Glaciers still hold consolidated snow cover; a later-season (2015) trip report found 'both Ruth and Icy glacier ... down to bare ice,' making the crossings harder and more exposed.

Mid-July through mid-September is the realistic window. Earlier and the long Constance Pass approach still holds snow and the buttress ledges are iced or verglassed; later and autumn Pacific fronts return, which on this range means days of low cloud that make route-finding on the face impractical. The most stable spell is usually late July into August, when the Pacific high suppresses precipitation over the Olympics. Even then, plan around cloud rather than around rain — the most useful piece of beta on record is that cloud cover, as always in the Olympics, makes viewing the route very difficult.

Late spring to early summer (roughly June through early July), while snow and ice still cover the crux chimney and the approach glaciers remain well-bridged; with no road access to Mowich Lake since the April 2025 bridge closure, the White River approach is the practical way in.

beta: A January 2002 ascent recorded as 'Lichtenberg Mountain West Face 5.9+' was made by James Nakagami, climbing with Dan 'Danimal' Capellini and a third partner. The wall sits just above Lake Valhalla; the approach is a short walk from the Smithbrook trailhead of about an hour, and it is an easier walk in than Snow Creek Wall — the implicit pitch for the crag. A 'grand west face' is separately listed as one of the mountain's three distinct routes, and a party is on record as having been turned around by the sheer wall before eventually reaching the summit by an easier line, which corroborates that this is genuine roped terrain rather than a scramble. Beyond the grade, the location and the approach, the beta is thin: no topo, pitch count, rack list or descent description is available. Anyone going should expect to do their own reconnaissance from Lake Valhalla, and plan for a full trad rack and a walk-off.

best_season: Documented as a January ski-mountaineering ascent as well as a standard-route summer scramble; outside of roughly June-October, expect a long unplowed-road approach (the 2019 winter party skied 8 miles of unplowed road plus 4 more miles of trail-breaking just to reach the trailhead area).

best_season: Mid-July through August is the sweet spot: enough of the Borealis Glacier's snowpack remains to bridge crevasses solidly, but the approach trail is snow-free. By late September the glacier is largely bare and thin — a Sept. 2012 attempt found the standard east ridge 'nothing more than a walk' unavailable due to conditions at Lucky Pass, with bullet ice and loose rock instead.

Trip reports favor mid-to-late summer through fall. An early-July ascent (July 2010) found lingering snow and a 'frigid summit,' so early season can still be wintry at this elevation. Multiple trip reports specifically recommend visiting around larch season (roughly late September) for more stable weather, drier talus, and better scenery; plan for the route to be most straightforward roughly August through October.
Late August/early September gives the driest moat crossing and best rock conditions per on-the-ground trip reports; earlier in the season the moat can be harder or more hazardous to cross.

Most commonly climbed as a dry-season scramble from July through September, when the route is mostly snow-free talus and trail. It is also a popular spring snow climb in late April through May/early June, when consolidated snow fills the approach gullies and col, allowing efficient booting/step-kicking (crampons and ice axe recommended, especially for a firm-snow descent); trip reports from this window note 12-18 inches of soft snow over a firm base and cornice/slough hazard near the Rock Mountain col.
